claim: A dry seed is dormant and can be stored for years; contact with water starts germination, and the enzymes inside the seed convert stored nutrients into a form the growing plant can use.
notes: Mechanism.

claim: Milled flour can no longer sprout, but the enzymes that trigger sprouting remain present, so milling at too high a temperature can damage some of them.
notes: No temperature threshold given.

claim: A recent study found that milling flour at home with a small mill had no significant negative impact on bread quality compared with flour from temperature-regulated large-scale mills.
conditions: home mill vs temperature-regulated industrial mill
notes: Footnote 1 of §2.1; sample size not given in source.

claim: Grinding grain exposes the seed contents, which is ideal for sourdough microorganisms, while the intact seed normally shields the germ from pathogens.
notes: Mechanism.

claim: Yeast and bacteria cannot make their own food; once the enzymes are activated, the food they need becomes available and they can feed and multiply.
notes: Mechanism.

claim: Amylase and protease are the two main enzymes driving sourdough fermentation.
notes: Framing statement for §2.1.

claim: Amylase breaks complex starch molecules into simple, digestible sugars; in the grain the germ uses amylase to convert starch into sugars for growth.
notes: Mechanism.

claim: Maltose freed from starch stays largely hidden inside the germ and is not consumed by the microorganisms on the grain surface until grinding exposes it.
conditions: whole grain before milling vs after milling
notes: Mechanism as stated.

claim: Higher temperature speeds up the amylase reaction that converts starch to sugar.
notes: Qualitative; no numbers given at this point.

claim: Amylase needs time to convert most of the starch into simple sugars; these sugars feed the yeast and the Maillard browning reaction in the oven, which is why a long fermentation matters for flavour and colour.
notes: Mechanism; author's conclusion is 'long fermentation is key'.

claim: Brewers keep mash at controlled temperatures so that the different amylases convert starch into sugar.
notes: Brewing reference used by the author to explain amylase temperature sensitivity.

claim: The iodine starch test (used in brewing) indicates unconverted starch when the sample turns blue or black after adding iodine.
notes: Test described as standard in brewing.

claim: Whether the iodine starch test works for bread dough is unknown; the author has not established it.
notes: Author speculation: 'I wonder if such a test would also work for bread dough?'

claim: Industrial bakers add enzyme-rich malted flour to speed up fermentation; if malt appears in a bread's ingredient list, this strategy was probably used.
notes: Author's explanation.

claim: Enzymatically active malt is not heated above about 70 °C, the temperature above which amylases begin to degrade; heat-treated inactive malt has no effect on the flour.
notes: Threshold stated as 70 °C in source.

claim: Protease breaks complex proteins into simpler proteins and amino acids; in wheat dough its main target is gluten.
notes: Mechanism.

claim: Adding water to flour activates protease, which in sprouting grain breaks down gluten to supply amino acids to the germ.
notes: Mechanism as stated.

claim: A wheat dough left at room temperature for several days can lose its gluten network: it tears, holds no structure and is no longer suitable for baking.
conditions: room temperature, several days (duration not specified)
notes: Duration given only as 'several days'.

claim: During fermentation a wheat dough becomes looser and more extensible, while the kneaded dough is elastic and holds together well.

notes: n=1 personal experience, not a controlled comparison.

notes: Author's reasoning; not measured.

claim: In a grain, most enzymes sit in the outer parts of the hull and are activated first when water arrives, which explains why whole-wheat flour gives a faster enzymatic response.
notes: Mechanism is the author's reasoning, supported by the cited source.

claim: Fermentation speed, governed by enzyme and microbial activity, controls crumb softness, crust colour and how much gluten remains in the final bread.
notes: Author's summary.

notes: Biology summary.

claim: About 1500 yeast species have been identified.

notes: Biology.

claim: Starter types are defined mainly by hydration; the choice trades off acidity, volume increase and the gluten strength of the flour.
notes: Chapter opening quote; also L23-L24.

claim: Regular sourdough starter is fed at 100 % hydration (equal weights flour and water, 1:1).
conditions: feeding ratio for the starter itself

claim: Liquid sourdough starter is fed at a water-to-flour ratio of 5:1 (500 % hydration).
conditions: feeding ratio for the starter itself

claim: Stiff sourdough starter is fed with half as much water as flour (about 50 % hydration).
conditions: feeding ratio for the starter itself
notes: Refined to 50–60 % in §4.4.

claim: With more bacterial activity, the microbes consume more gluten; so a free-standing loaf needs a flour with more gluten, because more gluten allows more of it to be broken down while dough integrity is kept.
notes: Mechanism stated by the author without a measurement.

claim: In a climate with weaker wheat flours, a stiff starter is advised because it increases yeast activity and reduces bacterial activity.
A liquid starter suits a very sour bread made with a very strong wheat flour.
Changing starter type is done only by changing the feeding ratio of flour and water; the microbes adapt over a few days of feeding at the same ratio.
Changes in starter type are usually visible after one feeding; 2 to 3 feedings, one per day, give a stronger effect.

The starter's microbial profile is carried into the main dough: more bacterial fermentation in the starter gives slightly more bacterial fermentation in the dough, and more yeast fermentation gives more yeast fermentation.
notes: Author notes this matters for an unfed, mature starter.

claim: A starter last fed about 48 h earlier has very active bacteria while yeast may be dormant; feeding can be skipped and a very small inoculum used.
For a starter fed ~48 h earlier, an inoculum of about 1 % of flour weight is the author's practice (10 g per 1 kg flour).
notes: Baker's % computed from the stated 10 g / 1 kg; the 1 % is the author's own statement.

claim: A very young starter fed only 6–8 h earlier may need up to about 20 % of flour weight as inoculum.
Remember that the dough is essentially a large starter; the dough's own response to the inoculum shows what to change next.
Flour enzymes break down starch and gluten over time; with a low inoculation rate (about 1 %), the starter can take about 24 h to regrow inside the bread dough.
notes: Author's statement; no measurement shown.

claim: A low inoculation rate (about 1 %) requires a stronger wheat flour because enzymatic breakdown of gluten may have degraded the gluten significantly before the starter regrows.
A wheat dough with degraded gluten flattens during baking and loses the typical fluffy crumb structure.
conditions: wheat dough with gluten broken down by low inoculum

claim: A stronger flour with more gluten allows a longer fermentation before most of its gluten is broken down.
The regular starter is kept at about 100 % hydration: equal parts flour and water; it is the most common and universal starter, with a good balance of yeast and bacteria.

claim: Whole-grain flour is the whole seed ground into smaller pieces; whiter flours have larger hull layers removed by mills and sieves.
Flour names describe which layers of the seed remain; the whitest flour is mostly the starch part of the seed.
In the German system a flour type number is the mg of ash left after burning 100 g of flour; T405 leaves 405 mg.
notes: Ash method as described by the author.

claim: A higher type number means more hull and mineral content, closer to whole flour, and generally a heartier taste; the scale differs by grain.
Across countries, the same flour name maps to different types: e.g. T405 (DE), T45 (FR) and 00 (IT) are the white-flour grades in each system; bread flour can be T405/T550, T45/T55 or 00/0.
notes: Table values as stated in the table file; read from tables/table-flour-types.tex.

claim: Grains such as rye, emmer, einkorn, rice and corn are homogenised only: no kneading, no stretch and fold, no shaping.
Spelt, like wheat with more than about 70 % wheat, needs homogenising, kneading, stretch and fold, and shaping.
notes: Table 5.2 lists 'Wheat (>70 %)'; the text says spelt contains significant gluten.

claim: Kneading builds gluten bonds, and the more you knead, the stronger they become.
During fermentation microbes metabolise gluten; if too much is converted the dough loses its wheat-like structure.
In low- or no-gluten flours the main fermentation concern is acidity (avoid an over-sour bread), not gluten degradation.
Bread flour (strong flour) has higher protein and gluten; it suits sourdough because the dough tolerates a longer leavening period.
notes: The author notes 'bread flour' is often mislabelled on packs; judge by protein/W, not name.

claim: The more gluten a flour has, the longer the dough keeps its integrity during fermentation.
For cakes a low-gluten flour is preferable, since strong gluten binding makes the cake chewy.

Germany grades wheat as A (good quality, can be blended to improve weaker flour), B (average, general baking), C (poor baking quality, e.g. sprouted; feed or biomass) and E (elite, only from optimal growing conditions).
The grade is usually not printed on flour packs; protein content can serve as an indicator of quality.
Large mills blend flours and blends are not labelled, so a pack's name does not fully reveal its properties.
The Italian W-value measures a dough's resistance to kneading; higher W means more gluten, more elasticity and a longer fermentation.
A high-W flour resists microbial inflation, so it needs a long fermentation; the long fermentation also lets microbes add flavour.
W 0–150: hydration about 50 %, very short fermentation, used for cookies.
W 150–250: hydration 50–60 %, short to medium fermentation, used for cakes, bread and pizza.
W 250–350: hydration 60–70 %, long fermentation, used for bread and pizza.
W 350+: hydration 70–90 %, very long fermentation, used for bread and pizza.
For free-standing sourdough aim for higher protein; low gluten makes the loaf collapse faster, so a loaf pan, skillet or flatbread is easier.
Properly damaged starch improves gelatinisation and water absorption in flour.
notes: Cited review: Wang et al. 2020, Food Chemistry.

claim: More damaged starch means more surface area, so water interacts better with the flour and microbes have more substrate to start fermentation.

Home mills often do not reach the starch damage of commercial mills; repeated short-break milling did not match commercial flour in the author's test, and home-milled dough de-gassed into flat bread in free-standing bakes, but worked well in a loaf pan.
notes: Author's own single-user trial (about 10 passes); generalised, no sample size.

claim: Bread types are classified by baking technique: flatbread (stove), loaf pan (oven), free-standing (oven).
Flatbread needs no oven, only a stove; it is the least effort bread type.
Flatbread can use any flour, including gluten-free corn or rice flour; adding a little wheat flour makes it fluffier because gluten traps gas.
A very wet flatbread dough gives a fluffier result because much water evaporates in the pan; very high water gives a pancake-like texture.
Flatbread recipe ratios (baker's %): flour 100 %, water up to 100 %, starter 5–20 %, salt 2 %.
notes: Flour = 100 % base; see table file. | auto-check: value(s) 0 not found verbatim in source text (unit conversion or derived)

claim: Pancake ratios (baker's %): flour 100 %, water 300 %, starter 5–20 %, salt 2 %.
Flatbread is ready when the dough has risen by at least 50 %; pancake batter is ready when bubbles are visible on the surface.
Feeding 1 g of starter with 5 g flour and 5 g water in the morning gives about 11 g of ready starter by evening (1:5:5).
conditions: starter refresh for a flatbread batch

claim: A warmer kitchen makes the starter ready sooner; in cold conditions use warm water.
Flatbread dough is typically ready after 6–12 h; more starter shortens and less starter lengthens the time.
For flavour aim for about 8–12 h of fermentation; too early tastes less developed, too late tastes more sour.
Timing is unreliable; judge readiness by smell: dairy, fruity or alcoholic notes versus vinegary (acetic) notes, which depend on the starter's microbes and temperature.
Cover the dough to stop drying and fruit flies; a transparent container makes readiness easier to see.
Chilling halts fermentation: dough that is ready early can go in the fridge and stay good for several days, getting more sour the longer it waits.
Fermentation is slower the colder it gets; a few cultures are adapted to cold, but a fridge preserves dough state.
notes: Footnote to the flatbread section.

claim: Tasting raw dough shows its acidity; it will taste quite sour, and the author uses this to judge readiness.
Skipping the starter build: about 1 % of older starter (flour basis) mixed directly into the dough makes it ready in about 24 h, depending on temperature.
notes: The author recommends 5–20 % in the table and suggests about 1 % for this variant.

claim: Using old starter directly can make the bread more sour because the balance of yeast to bacteria may be off.
For sweet pancakes add sugar at the end, just before cooking, so microbes do not ferment it; if added earlier, no sweetness remains after about 12 h.
For sweet pancakes, optional egg at about one egg per 100 g of flour.
Cook flatbread in a pan on medium heat with a little oil for even heat; dough from the fridge goes straight into the pan without warming up.
A lid over the pan cooks the top of the flatbread; the evaporating water circulates and heats the surface.
Flatbread should be about 1 cm thick; pancakes about 0.1–0.5 cm, depending on preference.
Flip the flatbread after 2–4 minutes and cook the other side for the same time; a longer bake gives more char.
Longer baking evaporates more of the acidity, so a too-sour dough can be balanced by cooking longer.
Flatbread: cook about 5 min per side, reduce time if too dark, extend if too pale.
Fermentation for flatbread takes 4–24 h depending on temperature and starter activity.
Wrapping cooked flatbread in a towel retains moisture and softness.
Store cooked flatbread or pancakes in an airtight bag in the fridge for weeks; if dry, spray with water and toast.
Keep some unbaked dough as starter; for later use add water and flour and keep it in the fridge, where it stays good for months.
Loaf-pan bread: mix, place in the pan, wait until roughly doubled, then bake in a non-preheated oven for about 30–50 min.
For loaf pan bread proof until the dough has roughly doubled in size.
Loaf pan bread is done at about 92 °C (197 °F) core temperature; a thermometer is the best check.
notes: °F value 197 kept as original.

claim: Loaf pan bread is baked around 200 °C (390 °F); free-standing around 230 °C (445 °F).
The loaf pan is baked at a lower temperature because edges heat slowly, so the top can overcook before the centre bakes.
Use steam or cover the loaf pan with another equally sized pan to simulate a Dutch oven, so moisture stays in the dough.
Loaf pan bread can use 90–100 % hydration; a very wet dough gives an airier, chewier crumb.
Replacing about 50 % of the flour with wheat helps the gluten network develop during fermentation and trap more gas.
conditions: loaf pan bread with other flours

claim: Grease the loaf pan generously or use a nonstick spray; do not wash it with soap, use a towel, since patina improves release with every bake.
Loaf pan dough takes under 5 min to work, and pans use oven space efficiently (several loaves per bake).
Free-standing wheat bread needs mixing enough to develop a gluten network before shaping.
Score the free-standing dough with a sharp blade before baking to control how it opens (the ear).
Free-standing bread requires gluten flour, an oven, about 60 min working time, and is the most difficult and costly type.
Flatbread: pan, fire or barbecue cooking, working time about 3 min, all flours, very easy, low cost.
Loaf pan bread: oven, working time about 5 min, all flours, easy, medium cost.
Flatbread dough made with einkorn is low in gluten, so it traps less CO2 than wheat; more water or some wheat flour makes it fluffier.
A wheat flatbread at about 60 % hydration is drier and harder to mix; wheat gluten lets it puff in the pan.
In pancake or flatbread bakes, pockets form from evaporated water and CO2 made by microbes.
Non-wheat sourdough uses non-wheat flour (all except spelt): mix, bulk ferment to the desired acidity, shape or pan, short proof, bake.
In rye, pentosans prevent gluten bonds from forming properly; with no gluten network, the crumb stays dense and not open.
notes: Cited: Buksa et al., Food Research International 2010 (wholemeal rye bread).

claim: Non-wheat flours (rye, emmer, einkorn) need no kneading, no stretch-and-fold, and no special handling for flatbread; over-fermentation is not a structural concern for them.
Rye loaf formula in baker's %: whole rye flour 100 %, water 80 %, starter 20 %, salt 2 % (yields 2 loaves from 1000 g flour).
conditions: rye loaf in a loaf pan

claim: Rye dough tolerates starter that is active or inactive, from a week at room temperature or straight from the fridge.

claim: A rye dough at 80 % hydration is too wet for free-standing shaping; lower it to about 60 % for free-standing loaves.
A stiff starter is easier to mix if first dissolved in the dough's water.
Rye flour is very sticky and hard to mix by hand; a spatula helps.
For non-wheat dough the mixing goal is only to homogenise and incorporate the starter; no dough strength is developed.
Rye bulk fermentation can last from a few hours up to weeks; longer fermentation raises acidity.

claim: Acidity stops rising after about 48 h of rye bulk fermentation because the microbes have used most nutrients; longer waits change flavour little.
Rye bulk endpoint: wait until the dough has risen about 50 %.
Dough tastes far more acidic than the loaf; much of the acid evaporates in the bake.
Rye dough is shaped by tucking, with no folding, and is shaped in a banneton; extra flour may be added to a drier dough.
The wetter rye dough cannot be shaped; spread it in a greased loaf pan with a wet spatula until smooth and shiny.
Rye proof about 60 min; a longer proof does not make it fluffier, though a short proof gives a more uniform crumb.
Rye dough can be proofed in the fridge, where it stays good for weeks.
Rye loaf is done at about 92 °C (197 °F) internal temperature; check with a thermometer.
notes: °F value 197 kept as original.

claim: Remove the rye loaf from its pan once it reaches core temperature, then finish unpanned with steam for an all-round crust; longer bakes give darker, crunchier crust.
Longer baking evaporates acidity, so a too-sour rye loaf can be softened by baking longer.
Wetter rye dough evaporates more water in the bake, giving a more open crumb; rye is never as fluffy as wheat sourdough.
Rye loaves are usually not scored; the crust cracks open on its own during baking.
Adding sourdough discard to rye dough can be done in any amount and gives a more complex flavour.
The crust of rye bread bakes pale; crust colour is controlled by baking longer.
No recipe can be followed blindly: adapt the formula to your local flour, tools and environment.
Mix the starter thoroughly into the dough so fermentation is even across the whole batch.
Kneading builds a strong gluten network, which is needed to trap the CO2 produced during fermentation.
Bulk fermentation is done on multiple loaves' worth of dough in one mass; the stop point is read from the dough's signs, not from a fixed time.
Divide the bulk and pre-shape each piece; this restores dough strength and gives more uniform loaves.
Proofing completes the fermentation and can be done at room temperature or in the fridge, depending on available time.
Steaming the dough in the oven gives oven spring; the second baking stage builds the crust.
The starter is the most important input: its yeast-to-bacteria balance is passed to the main dough, so an off starter makes the whole dough ferment badly.

claim: Flour, water and salt are the essential ingredients of wheat sourdough; additions such as seeds are optional.
Adding 20-30 % whole-wheat flour (of total flour) gives a hearty flavour.
notes: Author's preference.

claim: Whole-wheat can be used at 100 % of flour, but then use a strong whole-wheat flour milled from higher-protein wheat.
If whole-wheat is omitted, replace its quantity with bread flour.
Whole-wheat flour has higher enzymatic activity, so adding some speeds up fermentation.
Bread flour, with more gluten than all-purpose or cake flour, is recommended, especially for beginners, and is essential for freestanding loaves.
Salt is about 2 % of total flour weight.
Water for bread flour in this chapter's example ranges from 60 % to 90 % of flour weight.
notes: Range given in the ingredient example.

claim: Scale any formula by recalculating each ingredient as a percentage of total flour (baker's math).
Water need depends on the flour and is not fixed.
Whole-wheat flour, whose bran layers absorb water initially, needs slightly more water.
Water is absorbed into the gluten matrix as it forms; higher-protein flour can take more water.
Highly hydrated dough is more extensible (easier to stretch) and is used for fluffier bread.
Wetter dough stretches more easily and holds its shape for less time; stiff, low-hydration dough holds its shape longer.
Extensible, high-hydration dough inflates more in the oven, giving a bigger loaf with an airier, more open crumb.
notes: Author's car-tire vs. balloon analogy.

claim: High-hydration dough is stickier and harder to handle.
High-hydration dough needs longer kneading to build a proper gluten network.
High-hydration dough can become too extensible during fermentation and lose strength; stretch-and-folds are used to compensate, which means more work.
Shaping high-hydration dough is hard because the dough is very sticky.
High-hydration dough can stick to the banneton during proofing.
Over-proofing removes the dough strength needed to rise upward, so the loaf stays flat.
Wetter dough is more bacterially driven and loses gluten faster than stiffer dough; the starter must be in good condition to start such a dough.
Autolysis is used to shorten the main fermentation of wet dough, which would otherwise break down quickly.
High-hydration crumb can feel sticky; this is a matter of taste.
Raise hydration gradually: start at 60 %, knead until the water is absorbed, add more and repeat (bassinage).
By bassinage, a low-gluten flour was pushed to about 80 % hydration in the author's experience.
notes: One-off observation; flour and bake not specified.

claim: Keep adding water until the dough has the right consistency; the feel for it develops with experience.
Slow fermentation gives the extensibility of high hydration without very wet dough; slow it with less starter or a cooler environment.
Protease enzymes and bacteria both break down gluten, so dough becomes more extensible as fermentation proceeds.
Fermentation that goes on too long leaves little or no gluten; the dough then becomes very sticky.
A fast yeast dough (1 % dry yeast) is never as open as a sourdough dough, because protease cannot act in such a short fermentation.
notes: Author's observation from experiments; no numbers given.

claim: Industrial bakeries add active malt, which carries more enzymes and shortens dough time; malt is often an ingredient in supermarket bread.
A fermentation of about 1 h breaks down little gluten and gives a dense, not fluffy, crumb.
Very little yeast combined with a fermentation of at least 8 h (Neapolitan-style) gives a much fluffier, more open crumb.
The author's default pizza dough uses about 150 mg dry yeast per kg of flour (0.015 % of flour weight, computed).
notes: Percentage is computed by the extractor: 150 mg/kg = 0.015 %.

claim: Long fermentation (8 h or more) of yeast dough improves flavour and gives a crisper crust.
Amylases convert starch into simpler sugars, which brown better during baking.
The author's default hydration is about 70 % for his flour; the sweet spot is flour-specific and should be tested.
notes: Author's practice for his flour; not transferable without testing.

claim: Test each new flour's hydration capacity with a series of 100 g flour batches at increasing water levels.
Hydration test: five 100 g flour portions with 55, 60, 65, 70 and 75 g water.
After mixing until no dry chunks remain, rest the dough 15 min, then stretch it thin for a windowpane test.
Choose a hydration below the first mixture whose dough tears before a windowpane forms.
notes: Author's example: the flour mix could go up to about 65 %.

claim: Water is the cheapest dough ingredient; higher hydration lowers cost per dough weight but increases labour and failure risk.
Most bakers use about 20 % starter (by flour weight); the author recommends going lower, about 5-10 %.

claim: Autolysis extends flour-water contact and enables enzyme reactions that improve taste and dough characteristics.
The author does not recommend autolysis and prefers fermentolysis.

conditions: flour and water only, room temperature

claim: Enzymes sweeten oats when oat milk is left to rest (analogy for autolysis).

claim: Whole-grain flour speeds up the effects of resting because the hull contains more enzymes.
Prolonged enzymatic action tears the gluten network; the dough flattens and leaks the fermentation gas, the worst outcome for wheat sourdough.
At a 20 % starter dose and about 25 °C, fermentation can finish in as little as 5 h; a longer fermentation makes the dough leaky.
In that short 5 h, enzymes have not broken down enough flour: the dough is less elastic and too few sugars are released for flavour.
Enzyme reaction rates are assumed to rise with temperature until the enzymes are denatured by heat; the author has not seen studies on this.
notes: Author's stated assumption.

claim: Autolysis starts enzyme reactions before microbial fermentation; example: 2 h autolysis plus 5 h fermentation gives dough ready for proofing.
notes: Given as an example.

claim: Adding salt and starter to an autolysed dough is laborious and amounts to kneading the dough again.
Fermentolysis gives the same dough properties as autolysis without mixing twice: one fermentation of about 7 h replaces 2 h autolysis plus 5 h bulk.
For fermentolysis, reduce the starter from about 20 % (the conventional autolysis recipe) to about 5-10 %, or ferment in a colder place.

claim: Table of fermentation stages: a too-short bulk gives unbaked gummy areas near the loaf bottom and overly large craters; a too-long bulk gives a gummy-feeling crumb (most gluten broken down), many tiny evenly spread alveoli, and a flat pancake-like oven spring.
A perfect bulk gives an evenly baked, moist but not gummy crumb, evenly distributed alveoli without craters, balanced acidity (vinegary or lactic depending on the starter) and vertical oven spring.
A too-short bulk gives a pale, neutral taste; a too-long bulk gives a strong acidic profile that overweighs when tasting.

A recipe's stated bulk time is unreliable: differences in flour, starter activity and fermentation temperature shift the timing, and a 1–2 h difference can leave the dough under-fermented or over-fermented.

claim: Stretch and folds add dough strength during bulk; more folds give more strength, which yields a more aesthetic loaf with better vertical oven spring.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: For very extensible, high-hydration doughs, stretch and folds may be essential, otherwise the dough has too little strength to spring in the oven.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Stretch and folds homogenize the dough: fermentation heats some zones faster, so these areas accumulate more gas and acid; folding redistributes heat, gas and acidity and builds a more even crumb.

source.locator: Ch 7 Wheat sourdough §7.10 Stretch and folds > Homogenization; wheat-sourdough/wheat-sourdough.tex:L1037-L1044
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Very large crumb cavities can be reduced with more stretch and folds, but they can also come from under-fermentation (Fool's Crumb); check fermentation before adding folds.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Stretch-and-fold procedure in brief: wet hands with cold water, loosen dough from the container walls, lift one side to the centre and fold it over; rotate the container 90° and repeat, then rotate a further 180° and repeat once more, giving four folds in total.

source.locator: Ch 7 Wheat sourdough §7.10 Stretch and folds > Procedure; wheat-sourdough/wheat-sourdough.tex:L1071-L1091
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Procedure described in the book; the video referenced by the author shows the technique.

claim: Stretch and folds can theoretically be repeated as often as wanted, e.g. every 15 min; once dough strength is sufficient, extra folds only waste time.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Many consecutive folds tear the outer gluten layer; wait at least 5–10 min for the bonds to heal before folding again.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: If the gluten does not heal after tearing, the fermentation has probably run too long and the gluten has largely broken down.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Qualitative.

claim: Tighter shaping strengthens the dough, and more dough strength results in more vertical oven spring.
notes: Mechanism stated by author without measurement.

If shaping is hard to learn, make a larger batch, divide and preshape it, and practise on small batard rolls instead of one large batard.
notes: Practice method, not a dough formula.

claim: For a single loaf, apply flour generously to the top layer of the dough and rub it in by hand; for preshaped pieces, spread flour evenly over each piece's surface.

claim: Proofing is the final rise after shaping; the chemical and biological processes are the same as in bulk fermentation.
Shaping releases much of the gas built during bulk fermentation; proofing re-inflates the dough.
A dough that is not proofed has a noticeably less fluffy and softer crumb than a properly proofed dough.
There are two proofing options: room-temperature proofing, or cold proofing in the fridge (called retarding).
Some bakers say cold proofing improves flavour; in the author's retarded loaves he could not tell a flavour difference.
notes: Author's own unblinded tasting; no sample size given. Author states more research is needed.

claim: At colder temperatures the microorganisms work at a slower rate; the author doubts that cold changes their biochemistry.
notes: Author's interpretation; the 'doubt' part is his caveat.

claim: Cold proofing mainly helps manage the schedule: a dough shaped at 22:00 can be retarded overnight and baked the next day instead of needing about 2 h proof plus 1 h bake that evening.
notes: Worked example in author's text.

claim: After shaping, the dough can go straight into the fridge, proof overnight and be baked at any time the next day.
notes: Author notes exceptions covered later.

claim: Large bakeries proof dough a day ahead in the fridge, bake directly out of the fridge early morning, and have the first bread ready within about 2 h.
notes: Describes bakery practice as relayed by the author.

claim: Retarded dough can be baked anywhere from about 6 h to 24 h after it goes into the fridge.
notes: Text says 'as little as 6 hours later up to 24 hours later'; reference point (fridge entry) inferred from context.

claim: If an overnight dough is ready in the morning and you want to bake the same day, proof at room temperature rather than adding about 6 h in the fridge.
Choose room-temperature or fridge proofing according to your schedule and availability.
Room-temperature proofing is the easiest and most reliable method and works well for an overnight dough proofed the next morning.

claim: Use cold proofing (fridge) when you do not plan to bake within about the next 3 h.
A retarded dough first proofs at the same rate as a room-temperature dough and slows as it cools.
Fermentation stops when the dough drops below about 4 °C (40 °F); the exact threshold depends on the yeast and bacteria in the starter.
notes: Footnote says the actual temperature depends on the starter's microbes.

claim: A dough can rest in the fridge for up to about 24 h; in some experiments it was still good at 48 h.
notes: The 48 h statement is from informal experiments with no details given; confidence is lower than for the 24 h limit.

claim: There is a limit to how long dough can be fridge proofed; the author attributes it to continued fermentation at low temperatures.
notes: Author admits he can only explain it this way; no measurement.

claim: The finger poke test does not work on cold dough: low temperatures change its elasticity, so the dent never recovers.
Find the best fridge proofing time iteratively: try 8 h on the first dough, 10 h on the second, 12 h on the third, and so on up to 24 h.
notes: The 2 h step is implied by 'and so on' in the text.

claim: A fridge is typically at a constant temperature, so timings that work once can be relied on for later doughs.
A warmer dough going into the fridge takes longer to cool, so its fridge time has to account for the starting core temperature.
In warm conditions choose a shorter fridge proofing time; in cold conditions choose a longer one.
notes: Generalised from the author's seasonal practice.

claim: A pH meter measures the acidity that has accumulated in the dough, which can be used to control proofing consistency.
Test the pH at several proofing times to find the pH value that gives the best bread for your process, then aim for that value on every dough.
notes: Method, not a fixed value.

claim: Decision flowchart for proofing: room-temperature route: poke, wait 15 min, repeat until the dent is still visible after one minute, then score and bake. Fridge route: if baking within about 10 h, wait 15 min then proof in the fridge at 4 °C (40 °F); otherwise go straight to the fridge; bake from the fridge.

claim: Once the dough has finished proofing, preheat the oven to about 230 °C (446 °F) before scoring.
notes: Original: 230 °C (446 °F).

claim: Functional scoring is a small incision that lets the dough expand during baking.
An unscored dough tends to crack open at its weakest spots, which are usually where the edges were sealed after shaping.
Decorative scoring creates artistic patterns on the loaf.
Rub the surface with white rice flour before artistic scoring; it greatly raises the contrast of the incisions.
The ear is a characteristic that can be achieved on wheat sourdough with the right fermentation and scoring technique; it adds flavour and texture.
notes: Figure caption fig:the-ear (L1614-L1617).

claim: On a banneton proof, flip the dough onto the baking surface (oven rack, tray, stone, steel or Dutch oven) so that the side that was against the banneton now faces up.
notes: Pros and cons of baking surfaces are covered in the next chapter.

claim: Scoring at about 45° to the dough surface, slightly off the centre, makes the overhanging side rise more, producing the ear.
The ear is a thin crisp edge that is usually a little darker after baking and adds flavour and texture.
When scoring closer to one side of the dough, adjust the 45° angle so the ear still forms.
notes: Figure caption fig:scoring-angle (L1650-L1653).

claim: A razor blade gives a cleaner incision than a sharp knife because it is more flexible; it can be used directly or on a chopstick.
The scoring blade should be as sharp as possible so the dough is cut cleanly and not torn.
Rubbing flour on the surface before proofing dries the outer layer of dough, which makes scoring easier and reduces tearing.
notes: Figure caption fig:dried-out-dough-scoring (L1679-L1681).

claim: Cold-proofed dough is easier to score than room-temperature proofed dough because its low viscosity lets the blade cut cleanly; room-temperature dough tears more easily.
A ragged incision can prevent the dough from rising properly in the oven and makes the ear unlikely.
Practise scoring on a wet dough after developing its strength: the dough is sticky, so cut it, wait a few minutes, re-round it and repeat as often as needed.
After proofing there is only one chance to score the dough.
Placing the dough in the freezer for 30 min just before baking, once it is nearly proofed, dries the surface further and lowers its viscosity, making scoring easier.
notes: Author's trick; no measurement.

claim: Baking for 30 seconds without steam dries the surface of the dough further and makes scoring easier; experiment with the timing.
notes: Ambiguous whether the 30 s is before scoring or in the first oven phase; the text places it before scoring.

claim: During baking the dough's water and acids evaporate, gas expands, and the loaf rises (oven spring) while the outer dough sets into a gel-like crust.

claim: Acetic acid is produced by heterofermentative lactic acid bacteria and by acetic acid bacteria during fermentation; it gives a vinegary, sharp tang and lowers the dough's pH.
An aliquot jar is a small dough sample taken after initial dough strength is developed; it is used to monitor fermentation progress.
The aliquot's water temperature should match the room temperature, so the aliquot readings represent the main dough.
A small aliquot heats or cools faster than the main dough, so under large kitchen temperature swings it can misrepresent the dough's fermentation.
conditions: aliquot jar in fluctuating kitchen temperature

claim: A cylindrical aliquot container is needed to judge the dough's size increase properly.
In Germany, all-purpose flour corresponds to type 550.
Alpha-amylase cuts starch molecules into shorter fragments, producing maltose and some glucose.

The alveograph inflates a piece of dough like a balloon until it bursts, and the resulting curve describes the balance of dough elasticity and extensibility, used to judge a flour's baking performance.
Alveoli (crumb pockets) form when the gluten matrix traps carbon dioxide produced by fermentation.
Amylase breaks starch down into simpler sugars that feed fermentation; in brewing, the mash is held at set temperatures for an extended time so most starch is converted to sugar.
Autolyse is resting flour and water before the other ingredients are added; the rest activates amylase and protease, which shortens bulk fermentation and improves the final loaf's browning and crumb.
conditions: dough made with flour and water rest before other ingredients

claim: Autolyse is recommended when the starter inoculation exceeds about 20 % of flour weight.
Baker's math expresses every ingredient as a percentage of the total flour weight, which is 100 %, so recipes scale easily.
notes: auto-check: value(s) 100 not found verbatim in source text (unit conversion or derived)

claim: Example: for 500 g of flour, 60 % water is 300 g, 10 % starter is 50 g and 2 % salt is 10 g.
In the first phase of baking the dough's internal temperature rises and yeast activity increases, producing rapid carbon dioxide that causes oven spring.
As baking temperature climbs, the dough's proteins, mainly gluten, coagulate and set, which gives the loaf its structure.
During baking, starch absorbs water, swells and gelatinizes, which contributes to the crumb structure.
Crust browning comes from caramelization of sugars and the Maillard reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars; this also creates flavour and aroma.
Some acids produced in fermentation evaporate during baking; a longer bake concentrates the remaining acids less and lowers the tang.
notes: Author's wording: extending bake time makes acids less concentrated and reduces tang.

claim: Water in the dough turns to steam and evaporates during baking; the steam adds to oven spring and helps gelatinize starch.
The outer layer dries and hardens into a crust, which acts as a barrier that keeps the inner crumb moist.
A banneton supports dough during the final proof and is typically rattan or wood pulp; a bowl lined with a kitchen towel is an alternative.
While resting in a banneton, the dough surface dries out and becomes easier to score before baking.

In bassinage, water is added in stages: the dough is first mixed at lower hydration so gluten bonds form, then more water is worked in during kneading, which increases extensibility and suits lower-gluten flours.
After preshaping, a bench rest of about 10 minutes up to an hour lets the gluten relax so the dough is easier to shape.
Without an extended bench rest, pizza dough is too elastic to shape.
Beta-amylase breaks the starch fragments produced by alpha-amylase down into maltose.
Bread flour has more gluten and can therefore ferment for a longer period.

Brühstück is a German scald: hot or boiling water is poured over whole grain flour or crushed grains, the mix is cooled and added to the dough, which helps moisture retention and can improve flavour and texture.
Bulk fermentation is the first rise after mixing; a common target is about a 25 % increase in dough volume, which can then be raised to find the flour's best point.
Because the gluten (protein) content of wheat flour sets how long dough tolerates bulk fermentation, a higher-protein flour can bulk ferment longer; a longer bulk improves flavour and texture.
The best bulk rise is specific to each flour and has to be found flour by flour.
Low-gluten flours such as rye need caution with long bulk fermentation, since the dough can become too sticky, collapse and lose its shape.
The coil fold is a gentle stretch-and-fold technique suited to use throughout bulk fermentation; it improves dough strength while minimizing damage to the dough structure.
Diastatic malt is dried, ground malted grain whose enzymes break starch into sugars, which can improve bread flavour, colour and shelf life.
Dough hydration is the water weight as a percentage of flour weight; higher hydration gives a wetter, stickier dough and lower hydration a firmer one.
Example: 375 g of water with 500 g of flour gives 75 % hydration.
Dough strength is the dough's resilience and structure, which lets it stretch without tearing; it depends mainly on flour protein content and gluten network development.
A Dutch oven, a heavy lidded pot, traps steam during the early phase of baking, which helps create a crusty exterior.
Elasticity is the dough's ability to return to its shape after being stretched; it is governed by flour protein content and gluten network development.
Extensibility is the dough's ability to be stretched without tearing; it is the opposite of elasticity and suits open-crumb breads such as ciabatta.
Fermentation is the metabolism by which yeast and bacteria convert sugars into alcohol or acids; in bread it produces carbon dioxide that raises the dough.
Fermentolyse combines autolyse and fermentation: a small amount of starter, typically about 10 % of flour weight, is mixed with the flour and water at the start.
Adding starter early in a fermentolyse makes the dough more extensible and easier to handle.

After the final rise, press a lightly floured finger about half an inch (12.7 mm, converted) into the dough: a slow spring-back leaving a slight indentation means ready; a quick spring-back means more time; collapse or no spring-back means over-fermented.

claim: The float test checks starter readiness: a starter that floats on water has reached its peak and is ready to leaven dough, because carbon dioxide gives it buoyancy.
A starter that sinks in the float test is not yet ready, because fermentation has not progressed enough for good leavening power.
The float test is reliable for wheat starters but not for non-wheat starters, because gas escapes more readily from non-wheat doughs and they float less.
For non-wheat starters, judge readiness by bubbles in the jar and aroma; a mature starter smells mildly sour, not overly pungent.
A fool's crumb, with several large holes instead of evenly distributed small ones, can indicate uneven fermentation or improper shaping.
Gluten is a protein complex of gliadin and glutenin found in wheat and some other grains; when aligned and developed it gives dough elasticity and strength.
During bulk fermentation, much of the gluten is degraded by protease enzymes and lactic acid bacteria.
For einkorn and rye, where gluten alignment is not the goal, kneading homogenizes the dough into a consistent mixture.
Hooch, a liquid layer on a sourdough starter, indicates the starter is hungry and needs feeding; it acts as a barrier against mold and can be stirred back in or used for hot sauces.
A Kochstück heats flour or grains together with the liquid, and the mixture must be stirred while heating to prevent clumping and burning.
Lactic acid, produced by lactic acid bacteria, gives a mild, yogurt-like tang and together with acetic acid makes up the bread's acidity.
The Maillard reaction is a browning reaction between reducing sugars and amino acids that produces many tastes and aromas depending on reactants and conditions.
Maillard reactions occur readily above 150 °C and still occur, more slowly, below that temperature.
The optimal Maillard reaction rate is at pH 6.0–8.0, and the reaction favours alkaline conditions.
Maltose is a sugar produced when amylases break down starch; it is a primary food source for yeast during fermentation.
Non-diastatic malt is dried at higher temperatures, which deactivates its enzymes; it is used mainly for flavour and colour.
In a wet dough the flour's own amylases keep working well above 50 °C.
Flour amylases in a wet dough stay stable up to about 70 °C.
Flour amylases in a wet dough are inactivated as the dough heats further during baking.
Oven spring is the rapid rise of dough in the early oven phase, caused by expansion of trapped gases and water.
Over-fermenting wheat or spelt dough breaks down most of its gluten, making it very sticky; the bread bakes flat with many tiny pockets, as trapped gas diffuses out during baking.
If over-fermentation is noticed during bulk, place the dough in a loaf pan and bake it after a rest of 30 to 60 minutes.
pH measures acidity on a 0–14 scale, where 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.
Fermented foods with a pH below 4.2 are generally considered food-safe.
A pH meter can track a sourdough's fermentation progress.
The P/L value is the ratio of the alveograph's P (pressure, a measure of dough tenacity) to L (length, extensibility).
A low P/L value means the dough is more extensible than resistant, which suits products such as pizza or ciabatta.
A high P/L value means the dough has more strength than extensibility, which suits products that need volume and structure.
A preferment is a portion of the dough ingredients fermented before the final dough; examples are sourdough, poolish, biga, pâte fermentée and sponge.
Preshaping drags the divided dough pieces over the counter to make uniform dough balls, which makes shaping easier and more even.

Protease breaks proteins, including gluten, into peptides and amino acids; moderate activity makes dough more extensible, while excessive activity weakens the gluten network and gives slack, sticky dough with poor volume.
Protease activity rises with longer fermentation and with higher dough temperature.
In sourdough, the acidic conditions activate cereal proteases, and flour from sprouted or malted grains has higher protease activity.
conditions: sourdough and sprouted or malted flour

claim: Retarding slows the proof by placing dough in a colder environment, usually a refrigerator, which lets bakers schedule when bread is ready.
Some bakers say retarding improves flavour, in addition to scheduling.
Rye's low gluten content makes pure rye breads dense, so rye is often combined with wheat; pure rye breads are usually made with a sourdough process.
A scald pours boiling water over flour, grains or other ingredients and lets them cool; this gelatinizes starch, so the dough retains moisture and gives a softer crumb.
A scald may extend shelf life and inactivates enzymes that are harmful to dough quality.
A scald can enhance flavour and aroma and reduce bitterness in some whole grains.
Scoring cuts the dough surface before baking so the loaf expands freely and does not burst unpredictably; it also gives a controlled look.
A soaker is grains or seeds soaked in water for a set time, often overnight, before being added to the dough; it softens them and gives a moister crumb.

Tangzhong is a scald in which a small portion of flour is cooked with water or milk into a roux; it gelatinizes starch, improving softness and moisture retention, and the cooled roux is added to the rest of the dough.

Wild yeasts live on the surface of plants in symbiosis with them: the plant shields the yeast from pathogens and the yeast receives sugars from photosynthesis; when the plant weakens, the yeast can become parasitic.
The W-value, from the Chopin alveograph test, is the energy required to blow a dough bubble until it bursts and indicates a flour's ability to withstand fermentation and baking.
A high W-value means a stronger flour suited to high-volume bread and longer fermentation; a low W-value suits cakes and pastries.
Yeast ferments dough sugars into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat, which makes the dough rise.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Gluten also degrades on its own from the moment flour and water are mixed, because protease converts the gluten network into amino acids.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A flat loaf usually means the gluten network has broken down fully during fermentation; the dough is then a fully fermented food that may taste too sour and be less fluffy.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L432-L436
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L439-L443
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Only wheat- and spelt-based doughs can retain fermentation CO2 well enough for strong oven spring.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L443-L445
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A young starter that is not yet good at fermenting flour is a common cause of flat bread; starter performance improves with repeated feeding.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L447-L451
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Keep the starter at room temperature and feed it daily at a 1:5:5 ratio (old starter : flour : water) to balance yeast and bacteria.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L452-L456
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A stiff starter boosts the yeast share, giving less bacterial fermentation and a stronger gluten network toward the end of fermentation.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L457-L462
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A stronger flour with more gluten takes longer for bacteria to break down, so the dough can be fermented further before it becomes sticky and flat.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L468-L471
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: If fermented too long, the dough is broken down, becoming sticky and flat.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L471-L473
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Excess bacterial fermentation can be checked by taste (very sour), by a dough that suddenly becomes very sticky after a few hours of work, and by smell (should not be too pungent).

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread stays flat; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L475-L480
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Over a long fermentation the bacteria metabolise most of the ethanol produced by the yeast; they mainly produce lactic and acetic acid.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Lactic acid is chemically more acidic than acetic acid but is often not perceived as sour.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L489-L490
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: More tang is obtained mainly by a longer fermentation, which requires a loaf pan or a flour that tolerates long fermentation (a strong flour).

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L490-L494
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: For freestanding loaves a flour with at least 12 % protein is recommended for long fermentation.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L496-L498
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Generally, the higher the flour protein, the longer the dough can be fermented.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L498-L499
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Acetic acid is perceived as sourer than its chemical acidity suggests, so starters producing more acetic acid taste sharper.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L503-L505
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Strong acetic notes are favoured by a starter kept at about 100 % hydration.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L505-L506
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Based on the author's experience with his pure rye starters.

claim: Acetic acid production requires oxygen; a starter that is too liquid submerges the flour, limits oxygen and favours lactic over acetic acid.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L506-L511
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Acetic-acid-producing bacteria die out of a starter kept too liquid over time.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L510-L511
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Baking the loaf twice (about 30 min, cool, then 20-30 min more) gives a more sour bread because less acid is lost during baking.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L519-L529
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Observation from the author's micro-bakery shipping; the acid-loss explanation is the author's, supported by the cited sources.

claim: During baking, acetic acid leaves with the water vapour mainly from the crust, while lactic acid barely evaporates.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: After about 30 min at about 230 °C the crust is still pale and only part of the water and acetic acid has left; continued baking drives more acetic acid off with the steam.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L529-L534
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Source gives 230 °C (446 °F).

claim: Stopping the bake after about 30 min typically leaves a core temperature around 95 °C.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L534-L535
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: The crust darkens and gains aroma (Maillard reaction) only when the loaf is baked again after cooling.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L539-L541
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: The dough core does not exceed about 100 °C as long as it still contains water, so the crumb keeps most of its acids.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L541-L544
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: The author's sourdough stayed good for up to a week in a plastic bag, longer than a yeast-leavened dough that may mould after a few days.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Author's own experience; no sample size or conditions stated.

claim: Acidity in sourdough helps prevent pathogens from entering the bread, which supports keeping quality.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L545-L547
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Overly sour bread can be made more pleasant by toasting it, which boils off additional acidity.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > I want more tang in my bread; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L552-L554
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: For less sour bread, ferment for a shorter time.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread is too sour; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L558-L560
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Yeast produces CO2 and ethanol from sugars released by amylase; once sugar runs out, bacteria consume the ethanol, so acidity builds up with time.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread is too sour; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L561-L565
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: For the same volume increase, a dough with more yeast and less bacteria produces less acidity.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread is too sour; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L567-L570
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Feeding the starter once a day at room temperature shifts it toward yeast fermentation.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread is too sour; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L571-L573
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A stiff starter at about 50 % hydration favours yeast activity, giving fluffier and less sour dough for a given volume increase.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread is too sour; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L575-L580
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: In an informal balloon test with the same flour amount, a stiff starter produced more CO2 than a regular or a liquid starter.
conditions: regular, liquid and stiff starters, same flour

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: n=1 per arm, single baker, unblinded; balloons over glass jars; sample size not stated beyond that.

claim: Adding baking powder neutralises lactic acid and gives a much milder dough (author's unconventional approach).

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: If dough sticks while being removed from a banneton, transfer it directly into a greased loaf pan; the pan limits flattening, giving a less fluffy but tangy loaf.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread flattens out when removing it from the banneton; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L616-L620
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Measuring the dough pH before baking, with a pH meter, helps judge fermentation progress in later bakes.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread flattens out during shaping; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L636-L639
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Ciabatta dough tends to flatten somewhat after shaping.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My bread flattens out during shaping; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L634-L634

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: In humid tropical conditions the crust may stay crisp for only a few hours before turning chewy.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My crust becomes chewy; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L653-L655
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Storing bread in a container or plastic bag also makes the crust chewy.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.3 Bread > My crust becomes chewy; troubleshooting/misc.tex:L660-L661
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Toasting a slice restores part of its crispness; the author stores bread in a plastic bag in the fridge to keep moisture in.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: The crumb structure reveals how well fermentation went and flags technique errors.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Perfect fermentation; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L47-L49
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A honeycomb crumb needs precise fermentation: too long lets gas escape during baking, too short leaves too little gas to inflate the structures.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Perfect fermentation; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L70-L73
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A honeycomb crumb holds fillings such as jam better than an open crumb.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

notes: Informal tasting with family and friends, n=15-20; not controlled.

claim: Over-fermented crumb can be gummy because bacteria have broken much of it down.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L104-L106
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Over-fermented bread has significantly less gluten than the raw flour.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L115-L119
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: A too-sour over-fermented loaf can be improved by baking it longer to boil off acidity.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L124-L126
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Over-fermented dough can be used to start a new starter, or poured into a heated oiled pan to make flatbread.

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L134-L135

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L136-L138
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

claim: Safe fermentation length depends on the starter's yeast/bacteria balance: more bacterial activity breaks down dough structure faster.

source.locator: Ch 12 Troubleshooting §12.4 Debugging your crumb structure > Overfermented; troubleshooting/crumb-structures.tex:L138-L141
source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter

source.author: Hendrik Kleinwächter
